title: Designing the AI-first org chart
linkedinPost:
7% of companies have fully integrated AI across the organisation. (DesignRush, 2026)

For the other 93%, the blocker is almost never the model.

It is the org chart.

Traditional org charts map reporting lines. AI maps work. The two are not the same thing — and trying to add AI to an org chart that was not designed for it is why most AI programmes plateau at partial adoption.

The framework I use is called the Judgment Stack. Three layers:

— Automate: rule-based, high-volume, deterministic. KYC document extraction, transaction monitoring, report generation. AI owns it fully.
— Augment: AI proposes, human decides. Credit memo first draft, regulatory change summaries, onboarding risk scoring.
— Adjudicate: human owns fully. Credit committee sign-off, regulatory escalation, PEP review. Consequences of error are hard to reverse.

Every role can be decomposed against this stack. What remains in the human layer is a higher-judgment role than the one you started with.

What I would actually do:
• Run the Judgment Stack audit with the people who do the work — not just leadership
• Name a human owner for every AI system already running in production
• Set Revenue Per Employee targets by function, not company-wide — compliance and credit have different leverage points
• Wire EU AI Act and DORA audit logging into the same infrastructure as your human gates
• Run one deliberate Automate-layer migration before scaling

Revenue per employee rises when the org chart reflects the new division of labour — not when it treats AI as an add-on.

Full piece + the Judgment Stack I use for every AI org design engagement — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What is an AI-first org chart?

acceptedAnswer.text: An AI-first org chart maps roles and responsibilities around the distinction between human judgment and AI execution — not around traditional functional hierarchies. It starts from the work: what needs to happen, at what volume, and with what consequence if it goes wrong. Each task is allocated to automation, AI-augmented decision-making, or human judgment. Roles are designed around what remains in the human layer.

mainEntity.name: How do I redesign roles for AI without reducing headcount?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Judgment Stack audit separates the AI allocation question from the headcount question. Most roles contain tasks across all 3 layers. When AI handles the Automate-layer component, the person moves up to full-time Adjudicate-layer work — more judgment, same role count, higher output per person. Headcount decisions follow from the audit; they are not the starting point of the analysis.

mainEntity.name: What does the EU AI Act require from my org design in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Article 14 of the EU AI Act — alongside transparency obligations enforceable from 2 August 2026 — requires effective human oversight of AI systems used in regulated decisions. For financial services firms, this means every AI system in a regulated workflow needs a named human owner at the Adjudicate layer with the authority to intervene. This is a structural org design requirement, not a documentation requirement.

mainEntity.name: How does the Shopify AI-first model apply to a regulated firm?

acceptedAnswer.text: Shopify's principle — prove AI can't do a job before approving a hire — enforces role decomposition discipline: break the role into tasks, map each task to the Judgment Stack, identify what genuinely requires human judgment. In regulated financial services, the Adjudicate layer is non-negotiable under DORA and the EU AI Act. The decomposition discipline is correct. The conclusion is that you are hiring for a higher-judgment role — not asking whether you need a human at all.
